Another perfect nature stroll awaits when you hike the fairly-flat trail to Libby Creek Falls, which is accessible from this little-known city park at North Parole Street (take the Burke and Parole Street exit off I-280). A new informational board describes the geology, plants and animals living in this floodplain habitat. The board displays photos as well as lively accounts of connectedness among the creek with tides, plants, animals, insects, and more.

Learn to use senses and deduction to discover how light, water, earth and air work with plants and animals to create an amazingly complex community. Learn easily remembered reasons the leaves have color, how birds’ wings create lift; how nature disposes of waste. See why earth acts as a 100-rpm flywheel in the angular momentum dance that prevents our topsy-turvy Earth from swinging around like a weathercock. Details on how the cycle of light abundance to low abundance leads to changes in the Earth and other plants such as deciduous canopy trees, hemlock, spruces, grasses, clover, shrubs and ferns.

While learning how nature works to keep the upper Mississippi watershed alive and amazing, you learn tools to understand other ecosystems, and how human interventions knock out or replace the rhythms. How humans impact natural systems can then be decoded and acted upon to either help make things healthier or at best minimize damage that would take centuries to repair. Why for example apply fertilizers when the waste ‘washes’ away and merely fertilizes a completely disconnected ocean system, leading to a reduction of species in the watershed, while increasing species in a disconnected ocean ecosystem where light does not reach?

You are encouraged to find that out.

Most paths are dry and relatively flat; there are a few steep minor differences in height. The Interpretive trail is a 30-minute walk. The full hike takes 2 hours (or less, depending on the degree of “discovery”). Bring along water, an extra layer or two, curiosity and a willingness to see and feel nature at its most pleasant splendor in the hills of beautiful San Carlos. Parking is limited, on the edge of the woods on Parole Street, past the park’s parking lot.
